subject: ela
cluster: Research to build and present knowledge

items.prompt: Your class is creating a how-to guide called 'How to Be a Good Citizen.' Describe the full research process your class would follow, from choosing sources to writing the guide.
items.answer: Step 1: Brainstorm what being a good citizen means (helping neighbors, following rules, voting, etc.). Step 2: Write research questions: 'What do good citizens do?' and 'Why is citizenship important?' Step 3: Find two or three books or videos about community and citizenship. Step 4: Read together and take notes on the most important facts. Step 5: Sort the facts into a list of behaviors (help others, pick up litter, be kind). Step 6: Write the guide using those behaviors as steps, with an introduction and conclusion. Step 7: Revise and proofread together.

steps: Research process: brainstorm, ask questions, find sources, read, take notes, organize, write, revise.

items.prompt: A student says: 'Why do we need to research? I already know a lot about the ocean.' How would you explain why researching before writing is still important?
items.answer: Even if you know a lot about a topic, research helps you make sure your facts are accurate and find details you might not know. Books and expert sources have been carefully checked for accuracy. Research also helps you find new and interesting facts that make your writing richer and more informative for the reader.

steps: Research ensures accuracy.
Research uncovers new facts beyond personal knowledge.
Expert sources are more reliable than memory alone.

items.prompt: Your class reads three how-to books about making paper airplanes. Book A says to fold the paper in half first. Book B and Book C say to fold diagonally first. What should your class do with this disagreement?
items.answer: The class should try both methods and observe which one works better, or ask the teacher or another expert source. When sources disagree, testing the methods or consulting an additional source helps find the most accurate answer. For the class guide, they should explain both options or choose the method supported by the most sources.

steps: Disagreement between sources is common.
Options: test both methods, consult another source, or note both options in the writing.

items.prompt: Write a 4-sentence informative paragraph that a class could write together using these research facts: 1) Earthworms help break down dead leaves. 2) Earthworms create tunnels that let air and water into the soil. 3) Earthworms are eaten by birds and moles. 4) A single earthworm can move through the soil at about 0.2 miles per hour.
items.answer: Earthworms are small but very important animals that help keep soil healthy. They break down dead leaves into nutrients that plants can use, and their tunnels allow air and water to flow through the ground. Earthworms are also an important food source for birds, moles, and other animals. Despite their small size and slow speed of about 0.2 miles per hour, earthworms play a vital role in supporting life in the garden.

steps: Topic sentence: introduces earthworms as important.
Fact sentences: one for breaking down leaves, one for tunnels, one for food source.
Closing: ties together their importance and adds the speed fact.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a fact you find through research and a fact you make up. Why does this difference matter?
items.answer: A researched fact comes from a reliable source like a book, article, or expert. It has been checked and is likely to be accurate. A made-up fact is something the writer invents without checking. It may be wrong and will mislead the reader. Writing should use researched facts so readers can trust what they are reading. Using made-up facts is dishonest and can spread incorrect information.

steps: Researched fact: verified, accurate, trustworthy.
Made-up fact: invented, unverified, potentially wrong.
Writing requires accuracy to be valuable and honest.

items.prompt: Your class explored five how-to books about making healthy snacks. Now you are writing a class recipe book. Describe how you would organize the information from your research into a final written product.
items.answer: Step 1: List all the recipes and steps found across the five books. Step 2: Choose the best 5-10 recipes that are simple and healthy for kids. Step 3: For each recipe, list the ingredients and steps in order. Step 4: Write an introduction explaining why healthy snacks are important. Step 5: Write each recipe clearly with a name, ingredients list, and numbered steps. Step 6: Add a closing that encourages readers to try making them. Step 7: Proofread and publish the recipe book.

steps: Organize by selecting, structuring, and formatting the research into a usable product.

items.prompt: What makes a source reliable for research? Give two characteristics of a good source.
items.answer: Characteristic 1: A good source is written or reviewed by an expert or a knowledgeable author (such as a scientist for a science topic). Characteristic 2: A good source is published by a trustworthy organization (such as a school library, museum, or educational publisher) and contains accurate, checkable facts.

steps: Expert authorship = someone who knows the subject.
Trustworthy publisher = organization with standards for accuracy.

items.prompt: A class is writing a shared research report on how bees make honey. They have five facts: 1) Bees collect nectar from flowers. 2) Worker bees have a special stomach for carrying nectar. 3) Bees are yellow and black. 4) Nectar is deposited in honeycomb cells and evaporated to make honey. 5) Honey can last for thousands of years without spoiling. Which fact is LEAST useful for a report about HOW bees make honey? Explain why.
items.answer: Fact 3 ('Bees are yellow and black') is the least useful because it describes the appearance of bees, not the process of making honey. All the other facts describe steps or properties related to how honey is made. Fact 3 could appear in a report about bees in general, but not specifically in one about how honey is made.

steps: Evaluate relevance: does the fact answer the research question 'How do bees make honey?'
Appearance (yellow and black) does not explain the process.
Remove it from this specific report.

items.prompt: Write a how-to paragraph using three steps for a research topic of your choice. Include a topic sentence, the three steps in order, and a closing sentence.
items.answer: How to Plant a Seed: Planting a seed is a simple way to grow your own plant at home. First, fill a small pot with moist soil and press it down gently. Then, poke a small hole in the soil about one inch deep and drop your seed inside, covering it with soil. Finally, place the pot in a sunny spot and water it a little each day until you see a green sprout pushing through the soil. With patience and care, your tiny seed will grow into a strong, healthy plant.

steps: Topic sentence: introduces the task.
Step 1: First...
Step 2: Then...
Step 3: Finally...
Closing: encourages the reader or gives a result.

items.prompt: Explain why it is important to CITE or credit the source of your research. What does it mean to give credit to a book?
items.answer: Citing a source means noting where you found your information, such as the book title and author. It is important because it shows honesty — you are acknowledging that someone else wrote the original information. It also allows readers to find the same source and learn more. Giving credit to a book in Grade 1 might look like: 'In the book Wild Bees by Dr. Jane Chen, I learned that...'

steps: Citing shows honesty and allows readers to verify facts.
It acknowledges the original author's work.
In early grades, citing often means saying 'In the book...'

items.prompt: Your class is writing a shared research piece called 'How Rain Forms.' Write three research questions and describe what type of source would best answer each one.
items.answer: Question 1: What causes water to evaporate? Source: A science book about weather or the water cycle. Question 2: How do clouds form from water vapor? Source: A non-fiction book about clouds or weather. Question 3: What happens inside a cloud to make rain fall? Source: An illustrated science encyclopedia or a weather non-fiction text.

steps: Each question targets a different step in the rain formation process.
Match the source type to the content: science books for science topics.

items.prompt: Evaluate this research note: 'Bees are very important and we should protect them.' Is this a useful research note? Why or why not? Rewrite it as a better research note.
items.answer: This is not a useful research note because it is a vague opinion, not a specific fact. Better research note: 'Bees pollinate about one-third of the food crops that humans eat, which means that without bees, many fruits, vegetables, and nuts would not grow.'

steps: 'Bees are very important' is an opinion without specific information.
A good research note includes a specific, verifiable fact with measurable details.

items.prompt: Two students are doing shared research on volcanoes. Student A says: 'I found that volcanoes erupt because of pressure from inside the Earth.' Student B says: 'I found that lava can flow at up to 60 miles per hour.' How do both facts contribute to the class writing project?
items.answer: Student A's fact explains WHY volcanoes erupt (cause). Student B's fact gives a specific, dramatic statistic about HOW fast lava moves (effect/behavior). Together, they make the writing more complete: the first fact introduces the cause and the second adds a vivid detail about what happens during an eruption.

steps: Different students contributing different types of facts (cause vs. measurement) creates a richer piece.
Shared research works best when students find facts that complement each other.

items.prompt: Write the first paragraph of a class-generated how-to guide on washing hands correctly. Include an introduction, the number of steps, and why it matters.
items.answer: Washing your hands is one of the most important things you can do to stay healthy and stop germs from spreading. Follow these four easy steps every time you wash your hands: wet your hands with clean water, add soap and scrub for at least 20 seconds, rinse completely, and dry with a clean towel. Keeping your hands clean protects you, your family, and everyone you meet.

steps: Introduction: explain what and why.
List the steps briefly.
Closing: reinforce the importance.

items.prompt: Describe what a class writing project looks like from start to finish using the shared research process. Be specific about each phase.
items.answer: Phase 1 (Choose topic and questions): The teacher and class decide on a topic and write two or three research questions. Phase 2 (Find sources): The teacher brings in several books or articles. The class reads and discusses them. Phase 3 (Gather facts): Students take notes and share their best facts with the group. The class makes a list of the most useful facts. Phase 4 (Write): The class writes a draft together, using the facts to create a topic sentence, supporting sentences, and a closing. Phase 5 (Revise and edit): The class rereads the draft and fixes unclear sentences and errors. Phase 6 (Publish): The class writes or types the final version and shares it with an audience.

steps: 6 phases: topic, sources, notes, draft, revise/edit, publish.
